After substitution of \eqref{eq:c-cluster-expansion} into \eqref{eq:fixed-probe-centred-source} for $f= f_{\xi}$, each term, indexed by a family $\mathcal A$ of marked domains and an ordered list of $k$ cluster occurrences, is cut into its groups; the groups are pairwise compatible (roots in different groups are compatible as members of $\mathcal A$, clusters in different groups are compatible with each other and with the other groups' roots because the graph has no edge between components, and the intervals are disjoint by construction).

The regrouping is reversible: a compatible group family determines $\mathcal A=\mathcal A(\mathfrak B)$ and the multiset of cluster occurrences, and the term's graph has as components exactly the components of the groups' own graphs (no edges between groups, by compatibility), with the same hulls, so the classes and intervals are recovered; identical occurrences cannot split between groups because their domains are self-incompatible, so a group's occurrences are those of its term.

The ordered list of the term is an interleaving of the groups' lists, and the interleavings number $k!/\prod_Wk(W)!$, which turns the factor $(-1)^k/k!$ into $\prod_Ww_{\xi}(W)/\prod_W\Phi$-products.

The rearrangement is of an absolutely convergent sum: there are finitely many root families $\mathcal A$ at fixed volume, $|\mathfrak Q_{\xi}(\mathcal A;f_{\xi})|\leqslant \| f_{\xi}\|_{\infty}\prod_{D\in\mathcal A}\|\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f}_{\xi,D}\|$ with the total variations finite, and $\sum_{k}\frac{1}{k!}\bigl(\sum_{\mathfrak c\text{ hits }\mathcal A}|\Phi^{\mathrm v}_{\xi}(\mathfrak c)|\bigr)^k\leqslant \exp(\frac18\sum_{D\in\mathcal A}N_1(D))$; hence the term sum converges absolutely, and so does the group-family sum, being a rearrangement of it.
\end{proof}

A superscript $\circ$ denotes the reference data: the same $\Omega_1$, $\Lambda_1$, $I$, $J$, cubes, hosts, constants and cutoffs, with the background $U^{\circ}_1=\id$ on every bond, $V^{\circ}_0=\id$, zero retained field $A^{\circ}_{\mathrm e}=0$ and $\Psi^{\circ}_{\xi}=\id$; thus $H^{\circ}_{\xi}=\mathsf H^{\Omega_1}_{\id}$, the reference phase is $q_{\id}$, the reference primitives are those of Section~\ref{sec:source-phase-primitives} at $U=\id$, $f^{\circ}_{\xi}(a)= W_{\chi}(C;e^{iq_{\id}(a)})$ with the links off $\Omega_1$ equal to $\id$, and $f^{\circ}_{\xi}(0)=\chi(\id)=1$ since $q_{\id}(0)=0$. These data need not be a branch of the history sum.

Lemmas~\ref{lem:two-block}, \ref{lem:hessian-gauge-locality}, \ref{lem:row-locality} and~\ref{lem:primitive-sum} apply to $U=\id$ directly (Section~\ref{sec:source-phase-primitives}, opening paragraph; Lemma~\ref{lem:two-block} at $A=0$; the row solutions are those of Lemma~\ref{lem:charts} in its reference form, on the row polydiscs $\mathcal U_c$, and (B4) is not invoked), and the estimate lemmas used below (Lemmas~\ref{lem:regular-bounds}, \ref{lem:charts}, \ref{lem:gaussian-payment}, \ref{lem:activity-bounds}, \ref{lem:vacuum-clusters}) hold for the reference data by Appendix~\ref{app:background-estimates}, Lemma~\ref{lem:c2-reference}; in particular the reference near primitives are real on the open box (Lemma~\ref{lem:charts}: the analytic branches of the logarithms are real at real arguments, the row solution being real), so $K^{\circ}_{\xi;0}>0$ there and $I^{\circ}_{\xi;0}>0$.

Every lemma of Sections~\ref{sec:fixed-first-kernel}--\ref{sec:joint-extraction} stated on every branch (Lemmas~\ref{lem:walk-series}, \ref{lem:conditioning}, \ref{lem:component-blocks}, \ref{lem:polymer}, \ref{lem:probe-measures}, \ref{lem:measure-identity}, \ref{lem:grouped-source} and the first display of Proposition~\ref{prop:centred-expectation}) holds verbatim for the reference data: their proofs use only the field-independent geometry and the lemmas just listed. Every object of Sections~\ref{sec:fixed-first-kernel}--\ref{sec:joint-extraction} formed from the reference data carries the superscript $\circ$; in particular $K^{\circ}_{\xi;0}$, $I^{\circ}_{\xi;0}$, $k^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi}$, $\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}$, $w^{\circ}_{\xi}(W)$.

The index set of groups is the same for the branch and for the reference data: roots, cluster lists (the clusters are tuples of domains), contact sets and intervals are field-independent data (the sets $\mathcal F_{r_n}$ and $\mathsf L_D$ do not involve the background), and only the weights $w_{\xi}$, $w^{\circ}_{\xi}$ and the measures $\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f}_{\xi,D}$, $\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}$ differ.

For a group $W$ let $P^{\circ}_W(a)$ be the ordered product of the reference links along the consecutive traversals of $\mathcal H(W)$, in the cyclic order of the contour starting from the first traversal of the interval (for a whole-contour group, from the base point), the link of a traversal being $e^{iq_{\id}(\mathsf e_{\mathcal A(W)}a)(r)}$ when its bond $r$ is a bond of $\Omega_1$ and $\id$ otherwise, as in $f^{\circ}_{\xi}$ (oriented representatives inverted), with the integration variable $\mathsf e_{\mathcal A(W)}a$, zero off the labels of $\mathcal A(W)$; then $P^{\circ}_W(0)=\id$. Let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:part1-reference-group}
    a_W\coloneqq w^{\circ}_{\xi}(W)\int\chi\bigl(P^{\circ}_W(a)\bigr)\,\dd\Bigl(\bigotimes_{D\in\mathcal A(W)}\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}\Bigr)(a)\;.
\end{equation}

\begin{lemma}[Schur Identity]\label{lem:schur}
For $h\in G$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:part1-closed-schur}
    w^{\circ}_{\xi}(W)\int\chi\bigl(P^{\circ}_W(a)h\bigr)\,\dd\Bigl(\bigotimes_{D\in\mathcal A(W)}\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}\Bigr)(a)= a_W\chi(h)\;.
\end{equation}
Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:part1-reference-gas}
    S^{\circ}_{\xi,C}=\sum_{\mathfrak B\text{ compatible}}\prod_{W\in\mathfrak B}a_W=\frac{\int f^{\circ}_{\xi}(a)K^{\circ}_{\xi;0}(a)\,\dd a}{I^{\circ}_{\xi;0}}\;.
\end{equation}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For constant $u\in G$ let $(R_ua)_b\coloneqq\operatorname{Ad}_ua_b$ on $\mathfrak g^I$, an orthogonal map for the invariant inner product. At the identity background the constant gauge transformation $u$ fixes the background, so Lemma~\ref{lem:hessian-gauge-locality} gives $H^{\circ}_{\xi}= R_uH^{\circ}_{\xi} R_u^{-1}$; hence all walk coefficients, $C^{\circ}_{E_0}$, $\Gamma^{\circ}_{E_0}(\sigma)$ (the domains and weights do not involve the fields) and the Gaussian density \eqref{eq:fixed-kernel-density} are invariant under $(X,B)\mapsto(R_uX,R_uB)$, and $\mu_0$, $\mu_{C^{\circ}_{E_0}}$ are invariant. The cutoff factors are invariant because the bond norm is $\operatorname{Ad}$-invariant (\eqref{eq:marginal-cutoff-invariance}).

The reconstruction is covariant: by the intertwinings in the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:hessian-gauge-locality} at $U=\id$, $\mathcal N_{\id}\circ R_u= R^{(1)}_u\mathcal N_{\id}$, $h_{\id}R^{(1)}_u= R_uh_{\id}$ and $\mathsf C_{\id}R_{u,*}= R_u\mathsf C_{\id}$, so the unique small solution on the row polydiscs of Lemma~\ref{lem:charts} (reference version; the polydiscs are $R_u$-invariant because the bond norm is $\operatorname{Ad}$-invariant) satisfies $\widetilde D_{\id}(R_uA)= R^{(1)}_u\widetilde D_{\id}(A)$ and $q_{\id}(R_uB)= R_uq_{\id}(B)$, that is, every reconstructed link is conjugated by $u$; the primitives are invariant, being traces of products of links, Haar densities of conjugated phases ($\sigma$ is conjugation invariant) and determinants of conjugated operators.

The probe term transforms as $L_Y(R_u\lambda,R_ua)= L_Y(\lambda,a)$. Hence $k^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}(R_u\lambda)= k^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}(\lambda)$, and by Laplace uniqueness $(R_u)_*\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}=\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}$. Since the links are conjugated, $P^{\circ}_W(R_ua)= uP^{\circ}_W(a)u^{-1}$.

Let $\pi$ be the irreducible unitary representation with $\chi=\dim(\pi)^{-1}\operatorname{tr}\pi$ (the normalised character, $\chi(\id)=1$). The left side of \eqref{eq:part1-closed-schur}, as a function of $h$, is $\dim(\pi)^{-1}\operatorname{tr}(\Upsilon\pi(h))$ for the matrix $\Upsilon= w^{\circ}_{\xi}(W)\int\pi(P^{\circ}_W(a))\,\dd(\bigotimes\widehat\nu^{\circ})(a)$; by the invariance of the measure and the covariance of $P^{\circ}_W$, $\Upsilon=\pi(u)\Upsilon\pi(u)^{-1}$ for all $u\in G$, so $\Upsilon$ is a multiple of the identity by Schur's lemma, and $h=\id$ identifies the multiple as $a_W$.

For \eqref{eq:part1-reference-gas}, Lemma~\ref{lem:grouped-source} applies to the reference data (its sum converges absolutely, as shown there). Let $\mathfrak B\coloneqq\{ W_1,\ldots,W_m\}$ be a compatible family. If $m=1$ and $W_1$ is a whole-contour group, the reference Wilson function at $\mathsf e_{\mathcal A(W_1)}a$ is $\chi(P^{\circ}_{W_1}(a))$. Otherwise all intervals are short and pairwise disjoint; the groups are numbered in cyclic order starting from $W_1$, and by the cyclicity of the trace the ordered link product starts at the first traversal of $\mathcal H(W_1)$. The reference Wilson function at $\mathsf e_{\mathcal A(\mathfrak B)}a$ is then $\chi(P^{\circ}_{W_1}(a)\cdots P^{\circ}_{W_m}(a))$: a traversal outside every interval is outside every contact set, so its link is $e^{iq_{\id}(0)}=\id$ (or $\id$ by convention when its bond is not a bond of $\Omega_1$); a traversal in $\mathcal H(W_j)$ lies in no contact set of a root of another group, so its link depends only on $a|_{\mathcal A(W_j)}$, and the links of the consecutive traversals of $\mathcal H(W_j)$ multiply to $P^{\circ}_{W_j}(a)$ in the order of the product.

The integral against $\bigotimes_j\bigotimes_{D\in\mathcal A(W_j)}\widehat\nu^{\circ}_D$ of this character times $\prod_jw^{\circ}(W_j)$ is evaluated by Fubini one group at a time: integrating over the variables of $W_1$ with $h\coloneqq P^{\circ}_{W_2}(a)\cdots P^{\circ}_{W_m}(a)$ fixed gives $a_{W_1}\chi(P^{\circ}_{W_2}(a)\cdots P^{\circ}_{W_m}(a))$ by \eqref{eq:part1-closed-schur}, and so on, ending with $\prod_ja_{W_j}\chi(\id)=\prod_ja_{W_j}$. Since $|\chi|\leqslant 1$, $| a_W|\leqslant | w^{\circ}_{\xi}(W)|\prod_{D\in\mathcal A(W)}\|\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}\|$, and the sum in \eqref{eq:part1-reference-gas} converges absolutely by the bound of Lemma~\ref{lem:grouped-source}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Joint Extraction]\label{prop:joint-extraction}
For a compatible group family $\mathfrak B$ the joint defect is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:part1-joint-defect}
    R_{\xi}(\mathfrak B)\coloneqq\sum_{\mathcal S\subseteq\mathfrak B}(-1)^{|\mathfrak B\setminus\mathcal S|}\Bigl(\prod_{W\in\mathfrak B\setminus\mathcal S}a_W\Bigr)A_{\xi}(\mathcal S)\;,\qquad R_{\xi}(\varnothing)\coloneqq f_{\xi}(0)\;.
\end{equation}
Then, with $S^{\circ,[\mathfrak B]}_{\xi,C}$ the reference sum over group families compatible with every member of $\mathfrak B$,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:part1-scalar-extraction}
    F_{\xi}(0)= S^{\circ}_{\xi,C}f_{\xi}(0)+\sum_{\varnothing\ne\mathfrak B\text{ compatible}}S^{\circ,[\mathfrak B]}_{\xi,C}R_{\xi}(\mathfrak B)\;,
\end{equation}
and on every branch
\begin{equation}\label{eq:c-one-step-branch-identity}
    \mathcal J^{\mathrm a}_{\xi}[f_{\xi}]= e^{c_{\xi}}I_{\xi;1}\Bigl[S^{\circ}_{\xi,C}f_{\xi}(0)+\sum_{\varnothing\ne\mathfrak B\text{ compatible}}S^{\circ,[\mathfrak B]}_{\xi,C}R_{\xi}(\mathfrak B)+\mathcal B_{\xi}[f_{\xi}]\Bigr]\;.
\end{equation}
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Boolean inversion of \eqref{eq:part1-joint-defect} gives $A_{\xi}(\mathfrak B)=\sum_{\mathcal S\subseteq\mathfrak B}(\prod_{\mathfrak B\setminus\mathcal S}a_W)R_{\xi}(\mathcal S)$; after substitution into \eqref{eq:part1-grouped-source} and summation over $\mathfrak B\supseteq\mathcal S$, the families $\mathfrak B\setminus\mathcal S$ range over the group families compatible with every member of $\mathcal S$, giving $S^{\circ,[\mathcal S]}_{\xi,C}$.

The interchange of the sums is justified by absolute convergence. Let $\beta_W=(| w_{\xi}(W)|+| w^{\circ}_{\xi}(W)|)\prod_{D\in\mathcal A(W)}\max(\|\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f}_{\xi,D}\|,\|\widehat\nu^{\mathrm f,\circ}_{\xi,D}\|)$; then $| a_W|\leqslant \beta_W$, $| A_{\xi}(\mathcal S)|\leqslant \| f_{\xi}\|_{\infty}\prod_{W\in\mathcal S}\beta_W$ and $| R_{\xi}(\mathcal S)|\leqslant \| f_{\xi}\|_{\infty}\prod_{W\in\mathcal S}2\beta_W$. The sum $\sum_W\beta_W$ over all groups is finite: a group is determined by its root family, its cluster list and its interval, there are finitely many root families at fixed volume, and $\sum_{W\, | \,\mathcal A(W)=\mathcal A}| w_{\xi}(W)|\leqslant \exp(\frac18\sum_{D\in\mathcal A}N_1(D))$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:vacuum-clusters}, likewise for $w^{\circ}_{\xi}$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:c2-reference}.

A compatible group family has at most $N_{\mathrm m}$ members, the number of marked domains (its roots are pairwise distinct marked domains), so $\sum_{\mathfrak B}\sum_{\mathcal S\subseteq\mathfrak B}\prod_{W\in\mathfrak B\setminus\mathcal S}| a_W|\,| R_{\xi}(\mathcal S)|\leqslant \| f_{\xi}\|_{\infty}\sum_{\mathfrak B}\prod_{W\in\mathfrak B}3\beta_W\leqslant \| f_{\xi}\|_{\infty}\sum_{n\leqslant N_{\mathrm m}}\bigl(3\sum_W\beta_W\bigr)^n<\infty$; in particular $S^{\circ}_{\xi,C}$ and every $S^{\circ,[\mathcal S]}_{\xi,C}$ converge absolutely.

The second identity is \eqref{eq:c-physical-numerator} with $f= f_{\xi}$.
\end{proof}

At the reference data every nonempty defect vanishes: there $A^{\circ}_{\xi}(\mathcal S)=\prod_{W\in\mathcal S}a_W$ for every compatible $\mathcal S$ (proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:schur}), so $R^{\circ}_{\xi}(\mathfrak B)=\prod_{W\in\mathfrak B}a_W\sum_{\mathcal S\subseteq\mathfrak B}(-1)^{|\mathfrak B\setminus\mathcal S|}=0$ for $\mathfrak B\ne\varnothing$.

\begin{lemma}[Covered Branches]\label{lem:covered}
A branch $\xi$ is covered when every bond of the contour is a bond of $\Omega_1$ and every free-input stencil $F_{\gamma}$ of the contour \eqref{eq:native-source-arc-stencils} lies in $I$, that is, $\mathcal F_r\subseteq I$ for every contour bond $r$, with $\mathcal F_r$ of \eqref{eq:regular-stencil-extension-support}. On a covered branch $U_{\xi}(0)(r)= U_1(r)$ for every contour bond $r$, hence $f_{\xi}(0)= W_{\chi}(C;U_1)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
At $a=0$ the free vector is $B=\Psi_{\xi}(A_{\mathrm e})$, which vanishes on $I$. For a contour bond $r$, a bond of $\Omega_1$ on a covered branch, $U_{\xi}(0)(r)= e^{iq_U(B)(r)}U_1(r)$ by \eqref{eq:c-reconstructed-field}, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:row-locality} $q_U(B)(r)$ depends on $B|_{\mathcal F_r}$ only and vanishes when $B|_{\mathcal F_r}=0$ (for a free bond directly, for $r= b_0(c)$ because $\mathcal F_r=\mathcal E_c\cap E_*$). Since $\mathcal F_r\subseteq I$ on a covered branch, $U_{\xi}(0)= U_1$ on the contour.
\end{proof}

Appendix~\ref{app:background-estimates} proves Lemmas~\ref{lem:regular-bounds}, \ref{lem:charts}, \ref{lem:gaussian-payment}, \ref{lem:activity-bounds} and \ref{lem:vacuum-clusters}, and Lemma~\ref{lem:c2-reference} there transfers them to the reference data; Appendix~\ref{app:exterior-chessboard} bounds $\mathcal B_{\xi}[f_{\xi}]$ and the uncovered branches; Appendix~\ref{app:regional-scalar} identifies $S^{\circ}_{\xi,C}$ at the carrier $I$ with the flat coefficient $\kappa_Ce^{E^{\circ}_{\xi}}$, Appendix~\ref{app:signed-defects} bounds the defects, and Section~\ref{sec:leading-moment} bounds the history average of $e^{| E^{\circ}_{\xi}|}$.

\section{The Flat Regular-Region Calculation}
\label{sec:flat}

This section evaluates the first step at the identity background on an all-regular periodic lattice; Section~\ref{sec:regional-identification} treats a proper conditional integration region.

The group is in its fixed faithful unitary realisation $G\subset U(N)$, its Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$ is identified with Hermitian matrices, so that its group exponential is $e^{iX}$, $\tr_N= N^{-1}\operatorname{Tr}$, and the real inner product is $\langle X,Y\rangle=\tr_N(XY)$. The observable is \eqref{eq:wilson-definition}, with the normalised character $\chi(\id)=1$, and $d=\dim\mathfrak g$.

The first derivative of $\chi$ vanishes: the trace of its Lie algebra representation vanishes on commutators, and a semisimple Lie algebra is its own commutator algebra.

\subsection{The Covariance and the Normalised Insertion}

The operators of this section are in fine-lattice units. Let $E$ be the positively oriented bonds of $T$, let $T^{(1)}$ be its coarse centres, and let $E_1$ be the positively oriented coarse bonds. The blocking factor is the odd $L>11$ used by Ba{\l}aban (\cite[p.~251]{BalabanRG1}; the lemmas of this paper that need only $L\geqslant 3$ are stated so). For the covariance bounds below, $T=\prod_{\mu=1}^4(\mathbb Z/N_{\mu}\mathbb Z)$ with $N_{\mu}= LK_{\mu}$ and $K_{\mu}\geqslant 3$.

The block $\mathcal B_y$ consists of the fine sites at displacement $n$ from $y\in T^{(1)}$, with $n\in\mathbb Z^4$ and $| n_{\mu}|\leqslant (L-1)/2$ in each direction. For $x\in\mathcal B_y$, the path family $\mathcal G(y,x)$ traverses each nonzero coordinate displacement in one uninterrupted run, in every ordering of those runs; the path is empty for $x= y$. These are the centred blocks and path family of \cite[Section~0]{BalabanRG1}.

The averaging operation is \eqref{eq:global-average}; the formula below is \cite[(0.4)]{BalabanRG1}, its value on the set $\mathcal O_c$ where every logarithm has its argument in the chart domain (Lemma~\ref{lem:global-average}). \cite[p.~243]{BalabanCRE} permits this choice in the paragraph following (0.1).

For a positive coarse bond $c=(y,y+Le_{\mu})$ and $x\in\mathcal B_y$, let $x'\coloneqq x+Le_{\mu}$. The vectors $e_{\mu}$ are the fine-lattice unit vectors, $[x,x']$ is the straight fine path, and $P_c(U)$ is the transport along the straight fine path from $c_-$ to $c_+$. On the regular logarithm domain, \cite[(0.4)]{BalabanRG1} is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonlinear-average}
    \begin{aligned}
        \beta_c(U)&\coloneqq L^{-4}\sum_{x\in \mathcal B_{c_-}}
            \frac{1}{|\mathcal G(c_-,x)|\,|\mathcal G(c_+,x')|}
            \sum_{\substack{\gamma\in \mathcal G(c_-,x)\\
                \gamma'\in \mathcal G(c_+,x')}}
            \frac{1}{i}\log\left(
                U(\gamma)U([x,x'])U(\gamma')^{-1}P_c(U)^{-1}
                \right)\;,\\
        M(U,c)&= e^{i\beta_c(U)}P_c(U)\qquad(U\in\mathcal O_c)\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Every logarithm is applied to a closed relative transport based at $c_-$. The logarithmic constraint map and its derivative are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:constraint-primitive}
    \mathcal Q(q)\coloneqq\frac{1}{i}\log M(e^{iq}),
    \qquad Q\coloneqq\frac{1}{L}D\mathcal Q(0),
    \qquad \mathcal N(q)\coloneqq\mathcal Q(q)-LQq\;.
\end{equation}
The maps $\mathcal Q$ and $\mathcal N$ take a neighbourhood of zero in $\mathfrak g^E$ to $\mathfrak g^{E_1}$.

The designated bond $b_0(c)$ is the fine bond on the straight coarse bond $c$ crossing between its two blocks. Let $E_0\coloneqq\{ b_0(c)\, | \,c\in E_1\}$ and $E_*= E\setminus E_0$, let $\iota_0$ and $\iota_*$ extend fields on these two label sets by zero to $E$, and let $Q_0\coloneqq Q\iota_0$. The designated coefficient matrix $Q_0$ is invertible in this regular construction. The maps are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:constraint-extension}
    h\coloneqq\frac{1}{L}\iota_0Q_0^{-1},
    \qquad
    \mathsf C\coloneqq(I-\iota_0Q_0^{-1}Q)\iota_*\;.
\end{equation}
Thus $h \colon \mathfrak g^{E_1}\to\mathfrak g^E$, $\mathsf C \colon \mathfrak g^{E_*}\to\mathfrak g^E$, $LQh= I$ and $Q\mathsf C=0$. The free variable is $B\in\mathfrak g^{E_*}$, and $\mathsf C B$ agrees with $B$ on $E_*$. These are the designated-bond construction in \cite{BalabanRG1} following (2.10) and the elimination in \cite[(1.14)--(1.15)]{BalabanCRE}.

The gauge-fixing functional is the exponential one in \cite[(1.7)]{BalabanCRE}, not a delta-function axial gauge. For the transports along $\mathcal G(y,x)$, let $\mathcal U_U(y,x)$ be their local group mean: it is the unique solution near their diagonal value of
\begin{equation}
    \sum_{\gamma\in\mathcal G(y,x)}
        \log\bigl(U(\gamma)\mathcal U_U(y,x)^{-1}\bigr)=0\;.
\end{equation}
This is \cite[(0.10)--(0.11)]{BalabanRG1}. The gauge-fixing functional and the action used in the constrained reference integral are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:action-primitive}
    \begin{aligned}
        \mathscr G(U)&\coloneqq\sum_{y\in T^{(1)}}
            \sum_{x\in\mathcal B_y\setminus\{ y\}}
                (1-\operatorname{Re}\tr_N\mathcal U_U(y,x))\;,\\
        \mathscr A(U)&\coloneqq S(U)+\mathscr G(U)\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Here $\partial p$ is the oriented boundary of the plaquette $p$. All group means and logarithms are used in the regular chart containing the identity.

For $a,b\in\mathfrak g^E$, the flat Hessian is defined by
\begin{equation}
    \langle a,\Delta_1b\rangle
        \coloneqq\left.\frac{\partial^2}{\partial s\,\partial t}
            \mathscr A(e^{i(sa+tb)})\right|_{s= t=0}\;.
\end{equation}
The first derivative is zero at the identity. This is the $J_1=0$ specialisation of \cite[(1.16)]{BalabanCRE}.

\cite[(1.12)]{BalabanCRE} states strict positivity of the second differential at the regular constrained minimum. With the exponential gauge fixing and the constrained extension above, it makes the quadratic form on the finite free carrier strictly positive. The quadratic form and its inverse on that carrier are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flat-covariance}
    \mathsf H\coloneqq\mathsf C^*\Delta_1\mathsf C,
    \qquad \mathsf K_B\coloneqq\mathsf H^{-1},
    \qquad \mathsf K\coloneqq\mathsf C\mathsf K_B\mathsf C^*\;.
\end{equation}
The adjoint and Lebesgue measure use the stated real inner products, summed over the respective bond labels. Thus $\mathsf K$ is the covariance of the linearised fine field $\mathsf C B$.

The normalised Gaussian measure on the free carrier is denoted by $\mu_{\mathsf K_B}$. In an orthonormal basis of real dimension $D= d| E_*|$, it has density
\begin{equation}
    \dd\mu_{\mathsf K_B}(B)
        =(2\pi)^{-D/2}(\det\mathsf K_B)^{-1/2}
            e^{-\frac{1}{2}\langle B,\mathsf H B\rangle}\,\dd B\;.
\end{equation}

Ba{\l}aban's nonlinear constraint solution gives the fine phase
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flat-phase}
    q_{g_0}(B)= g_0\mathsf C B-h\widetilde D(g_0\mathsf C B),
    \qquad U_{g_0}(b)= e^{iq_{g_0}(B)(b)}\;.
\end{equation}
The correction $\widetilde D \colon \mathfrak g^E\to\mathfrak g^{E_1}$ is defined near zero by the unique small analytic solution
\begin{equation}
    \widetilde D(A)=\mathcal N(A-h\widetilde D(A)),
    \qquad \widetilde D(0)=0\;.
\end{equation}
Its construction is that of \cite{BalabanRG1} following (2.10). Since $\mathcal N(0)= D\mathcal N(0)=0$, its expansion starts at degree two. Equation~\eqref{eq:flat-phase} therefore solves the nonlinear averaging constraint and has $q_{g_0}(B)= g_0\mathsf C B+O(g_0^2)$ at fixed $B$.

For a fixed $\sigma\in \{\mathrm{op},\mathrm{HS}\}$, the corresponding matrix norm is used for both group-matrix and Lie-algebra cutoff tests:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-two-norms}
    | X|_{\mathrm{op}}=\sup_{| v|_2=1}| Xv|_2,
    \qquad | X|_{\mathrm{HS}}=
        \left(\tr_N(X^*X)\right)^{\frac{1}{2}}\;.
\end{equation}
Here $| v|_2$ is the Euclidean vector norm. The dependence on the fixed $\sigma$ is suppressed in $\vartheta_{g_0}$ and $\mathcal W_{g_0}$ below.

In the all-regular branch, $U_1= U_{1,\square'}=\id$. \cite[(1.19)]{BalabanCRE} removes the approximate relative-field tests on the good fluctuation cubes. The other retained chart tests in \cite[(1.25)]{BalabanCRE} have support in $S_1=\varnothing$. The guard statement following \cite[(1.10)]{BalabanCRE} removes the earlier plaquette and gauge cutoffs under its prescribed parameter hierarchy. With that hierarchy retained, \cite[(1.18)--(1.19), (1.25)--(1.26)]{BalabanCRE} gives the following bond product when its bond norm is read as $|\bigcdot |_{\sigma}$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:literal-cutoff}
    \vartheta_{g_0}(B)=\prod_{b\in E_*}
        \mathbf 1_{\{\,| B(b)|_{\sigma}< r(g_0)\,\}},
    \qquad r(g_0)= A_1(\log g_0^{-2})^{p_0}\;.
\end{equation}
Here $A_1>0$ and $p_0\geqslant 5\mathfrak r$ ($\mathfrak r\geqslant 2$ the logarithmic exponent of the macro-cube sizes, the convention of Section~\ref{sec:sourced-effective-interaction}; Section~\ref{app:thresholds}) are the first-step cutoff parameters, and $\delta_0= g_0r(g_0)$.

The normalisation is the inductive one following \cite[(3.4)]{BalabanCRE}, $\delta_k= g_kA_1/A_0\,p_0(g_k)$ as printed at p.265, together with \cite[(2.4)]{BalabanCRE}, also at the first step:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cre-cutoff-normalisation}
    \begin{aligned}
        p_0(g_k)&\coloneqq A_0(\log g_k^{-2})^{p_0}\;,\\
        \varepsilon_k&\coloneqq g_kp_0(g_k)\;,\\
        \delta_k&\coloneqq g_k\frac{A_1}{A_0}p_0(g_k)
            =\frac{A_1}{A_0}\varepsilon_k\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
For the first step this gives $\delta_0/g_0= A_1(\log g_0^{-2})^{p_0}$.

The application to \cite{BalabanCRE} assumes its compatible cube partitions and admissible first-step parameters: sufficiently large cutoff constants, sufficiently small $A_1/A_0$ and coupling, and $p_0\geqslant 5\mathfrak r$, where $\mathfrak r\geqslant 2$ is the logarithmic exponent defining the macro-cube sizes (Section~\ref{sec:sourced-effective-interaction}). Under these hypotheses the guard statement following \cite[(1.10)]{BalabanCRE} removes $\chi_0$ and $\chi_{Ax}$ in the regular region. The reference integral below is specified separately for each of the two matrix-norm prescriptions; its identification with a conditional kernel uses that same prescription.

Let $\sigma_H(q)$ be the density of normalised Haar measure in exponential coordinates relative to the stated Lie-algebra Lebesgue measure, and let $j_H(q)\coloneqq\sigma_H(q)/\sigma_H(0)$. The Jacobian and residual exponent are the pullbacks of the measure and the action:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:literal-residual}
    \begin{aligned}
        J_{g_0}(B)&\coloneqq
            \left|\det_{\mathfrak g^E}
                \bigl(I-hD\widetilde D(g_0\mathsf C B)\bigr)\right|
            \prod_{b\in E}j_H(q_{g_0}(B)(b))\;,\\
        \mathcal P_{g_0}(B)&\coloneqq\log J_{g_0}(B)
            -\frac{1}{g_0^2}\mathscr A(U_{g_0})
            +\frac{1}{2}\langle B,\mathsf H B\rangle\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The determinant is on the real fine carrier. The nonlinear change of variables is made before the linear constraints are eliminated, as in \cite[(1.14)]{BalabanCRE}.

The subsequent linear-constraint factor, Haar density at zero, coupling rescaling, gauge normaliser and vacuum scalar are common to the numerator and denominator in this branch. After the cutoff reductions above, \eqref{eq:literal-residual} retains the action, Haar and Jacobian factors of \cite[(1.14)--(1.16)]{BalabanCRE}, with the same exponential gauge fixing. Its constant coefficient at $g_0=0$ is zero.

The regular sourced ratio is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flat-ratio}
    \mathcal W_{g_0}(C)\coloneqq
        \frac{\displaystyle\int
            \vartheta_{g_0}(B)e^{\mathcal P_{g_0}(B)}
            W_{\chi}(C;U_{g_0})\,\dd\mu_{\mathsf K_B}(B)}
        {\displaystyle\int
            \vartheta_{g_0}(B)e^{\mathcal P_{g_0}(B)}
            \,\dd\mu_{\mathsf K_B}(B)}\;.
\end{equation}

\section{The Straight-Edge Coefficient from Gaussian Marginals}
\label{sec:marginal-perimeter}

The normalised flat integral has a connected expansion. Its extensive contribution along a long straight side defines $\delta m$; the contributions remaining near the corners define $z_{\mathrm c}$. These terms are constructed from Gaussian principal marginals and the local interaction \eqref{eq:perimeter-literal-local-sum}; Section~\ref{sec:regional-identification} compares the straight-side coefficient with the conditional kernel in a proper regular region.

For a square $C_n$ on the compatible finite torus $T$, the flat reference numerator and denominator are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:perimeter-native-integrals}
    \begin{aligned}
        N_{n,T}&\coloneqq\int\vartheta_{g_0}(B)e^{\mathcal P_{g_0}(B)}
            W_{\chi}(C_n;U_{g_0})\,\dd\mu_{\mathsf K_B}(B)\;,\\
        D_T&\coloneqq\int\vartheta_{g_0}(B)e^{\mathcal P_{g_0}(B)}
            \,\dd\mu_{\mathsf K_B}(B)\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
These are the identity-background regular integrals. In the two-norm construction below the cutoff is $\vartheta_{g_0}^{\sigma}$, and $N_{n,T}= N_{C_n,T}^{\sigma}$, $D_T= D_T^{\sigma}$ for the chosen prescription $\sigma$.

\subsection{Connected Terms of the Normalised Integral}

Let $E_*$ be the free-bond carrier and let $C_T\coloneqq\mathsf K_B$ on a compatible finite torus $T$. The flat gap and exponential decay proved in Appendix~\ref{app:flat-covariance} give positive constants $\lambda,\Lambda,A,\mu$, independent of $T$, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-covariance-input}
    \lambda I\leqslant C_T\leqslant \Lambda I,
    \qquad \| C_T(b,c)\|\leqslant A e^{-\mu d_T(b,c)}\;.
\end{equation}
For positive bonds $b=(x,i)$ and $c=(y,j)$, let $d_T(b,c)\coloneqq d_{\infty,T}(x,y)+\mathbf1_{\{ i\ne j\}}$, where the first term is periodic maximum-norm site distance in fine-lattice units. The same bounds hold for every principal marginal.

One may take $\lambda= h_L^{-1}$ and $\Lambda=\gamma_L^{-1}$ from \eqref{eq:covariance-uniform-gap} and \eqref{eq:bulk-uniform-gap}. The free-inverse Neumann series \eqref{eq:bulk-neumann-inverse} applies on the compatible tori as well, with the same gap and row-sum bound.

Let $d_{\mathrm{block}}(b,c)$ be the periodic maximum-norm distance between the coarse indices of the blocks containing the initial sites of $b,c$. The block-distance decay converts to the fine distance using $d_T(b,c)\leqslant Ld_{\mathrm{block}}(b,c)+2L$; decreasing the decay exponent by the factor $L$ and enlarging $A$ suffices.

The metric on each Lie algebra factor is the fixed invariant real metric. All constants below may depend on this metric, $G$, $L$, the fixed local reconstruction and $\chi$, but not on the square size or torus volume.

Throughout this construction, $r_0(g_0)= r(g_0)= A_1(\log g_0^{-2})^{p_0}$ is exactly the threshold in \eqref{eq:literal-cutoff}. Restoring the fixed norm index gives the two cutoff prescriptions
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-two-cutoffs}
    \vartheta_{g_0}^{\sigma}(B)
        =\prod_{b\in E_*}
            \mathbf1_{\{\,| B_b|_{\sigma}< r_0(g_0)\,\}}\;.
\end{equation}
The result holds separately for each prescription, with that cutoff retained in both numerator and denominator. With the bond tests of \cite{BalabanCRE} interpreted in the same norm, the regular-branch reduction above identifies its reference kernel.

For unitary $u$, the required invariance follows from
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-cutoff-invariance}
    \begin{aligned}
        | uXu^{-1}|_{\mathrm{op}}
            &=\sup_{| v|_2=1}| uXu^{-1}v|_2
                =\sup_{| w|_2=1}| Xw|_2=| X|_{\mathrm{op}}\;,\\
        | uXu^{-1}|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2
            &=\tr_N\bigl(uX^*Xu^{-1}\bigr)
                =\tr_N(X^*X)=| X|_{\mathrm{HS}}^2\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Thus each good- or bad-bond test is invariant for the same fixed norm and threshold; a supremum over the bonds of a cube and products of such tests preserve this invariance.

In the regular branch the starred carrier excludes the designated bonds, $A=\mathsf C B$ agrees with $B$ on that carrier, and $g_0^{-1}\delta_0= r_0$ by \eqref{eq:cre-cutoff-normalisation}. Repeated cube tests reduce to the bond product \eqref{eq:literal-cutoff} by idempotence, as in the stated regular-branch reduction.

The numerator and denominator are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-literal-ratio}
    \begin{aligned}
        N_{C,T}^{\sigma}&\coloneqq\int\vartheta_{g_0}^{\sigma}(B)e^{\mathcal P_{g_0}(B)}
            W_{\chi}(C;U_{g_0})\,\dd\mu_{C_T}(B)\;,\\
        D_T^{\sigma}&\coloneqq\int\vartheta_{g_0}^{\sigma}(B)e^{\mathcal P_{g_0}(B)}
            \,\dd\mu_{C_T}(B)\;,
        \qquad \mathcal W_T^{\circ,\sigma}(C)\coloneqq N_{C,T}^{\sigma}/D_T^{\sigma}\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}

In the proof $\sigma$ is fixed and its index is suppressed on the cutoffs, integrals, and cluster weights; $r= r_0(g_0)$ and $\vartheta_b=\mathbf1_{\{| B_b|_{\sigma}< r\}}$. Let $\mathcal V_T$ index the local terms $v$ in \eqref{eq:perimeter-literal-local-sum}, with supports $\Lambda_v$. The bounded measurable functions on the full real carrier are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-local-vertices}
    f_v(B)\coloneqq\left(\prod_{b\in \Lambda_v}\vartheta_b(B)\right)
        (e^{v(B)}-1),
    \qquad h_b(B)\coloneqq-(1-\vartheta_b(B))\;.
\end{equation}
The first function is zero where its cutoff vanishes, so the local analytic function is never evaluated outside its chart. On the original cutoff the exact identity is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-original-weight}
    \vartheta_{g_0}(B)e^{\mathcal P_{g_0}(B)}
        =\prod_{b\in E_*}(1+h_b(B))
            \prod_{v\in \mathcal V_T}(1+f_v(B))\;.
\end{equation}
For a square $C=(b_a)_{a\in\mathcal I_C}$, let $\mathcal I_C$ be its ordered finite traversal set and let $U_0\coloneqq\id$. For $R\subseteq\mathcal I_C$, let $H_R(B)$ be the ordered transport around $C$ using $U_{g_0}(b_a)$ on $R$ and $U_0(b_a)$ elsewhere. The closed source differences are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:finite-source-closed-differences}
    G_S(B)\coloneqq\sum_{R\subseteq S}(-1)^{| S|-| R|}
        \chi\left(H_R(B)(\Hol_{U_0}C)^{-1}\right),
    \qquad \sum_{S\subseteq\mathcal I_C}G_S(B)
        = W_{\chi}(C;U_{g_0})\;.
\end{equation}
The last equality is Boolean inversion and uses $\Hol_{U_0}C=\id$. Every summand is a closed contraction, invariant under simultaneous gauge transformation of field and reference. The identity-gauge representative is used to evaluate its flat reference integral.

A selected traversal $a$ has its fixed local free-input support $\Lambda_a$. Multiplying $G_S$ by $\prod_{a\in S}\prod_{b\in \Lambda_a}\vartheta_b$ leaves its contribution in the original cutoff integral unchanged. This product is zero off that protected box, so only the reconstruction rows selected by the mixed word are evaluated.

A label selection is $J=(D,P,S)$, with $D\subseteq \mathcal V_T$, $P\subseteq E_*$ and $S$ a subset of contour traversals. Its active carrier and scalar local factor are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-selection}
    \begin{aligned}
        A_J&\coloneqq\bigcup_{v\in D}\Lambda_v\cup P
            \cup\bigcup_{a\in S}\Lambda_a\;,\\
        F_J(B)&\coloneqq\prod_{v\in D}f_v(B)\prod_{b\in P}h_b(B)
            \prod_{a\in S}\prod_{b\in \Lambda_a}\vartheta_b(B)\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The corresponding numerator term is exactly $\int F_JG_S\,\dd\mu_{(C_T)_{A_J}}$. This is a marginal of the original Gaussian: its coordinates in $E_*\setminus A_J$ have been integrated out, while every interaction and cutoff is still present in the sum over $J$.

There are fixed integers $s_*,q_*$ and a fixed range $R_*$ such that every label support has at most $s_*$ bonds and diameter at most $R_*$, and at most $q_*$ possible labels meet any bond. $R_*$ is enlarged so that every bond in $\Lambda_a$ is within $R_*$ of the source traversal $a$; a reversed traversal uses the free-input stencil of its positive representative. These are consequences of the bounded overlap of the primitive supports and the fact that a square has no repeated traversal.

The source cutoff is inserted before expanding the full product of cutoff factors in \eqref{eq:marginal-original-weight}; an individual expanded term need not satisfy the full cutoff.

For a finite carrier $A$, let $C_A\coloneqq(C_T)_A$. With one scalar variable $x_{bc}= x_{cb}$ for each pair of distinct bonds of $A$, $C_A(x)$ keeps the diagonal blocks of $C_A$ and multiplies its $bc$ block by $x_{bc}$. For a forest $F$ on $A$ and parameters $w\in [0,1]^F$, let $w^F_{bc}$ be the minimum of the parameters on the unique forest path from $b$ to $c$, or zero if there is no path; its diagonal is one. Let $\partial_F\coloneqq\prod_{\{ b,c\}\in F}\partial_{x_{bc}}$. The Taylor forest formula gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-forest-identity}
    \int F_JG_S\,\dd\mu_{C_{A_J}}
        =\sum_{F\ \mathrm{forest\ on}\ A_J}
            \int_{[0,1]^F}\int F_J(B)G_S(B)
                \left.\partial_F p_{C_{A_J}(x)}(B)\right|_{x= w^F}
                    \,\dd B\,\dd w\;.
\end{equation}
For a covariance on $\mathfrak g^A$, the density used here is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-density-definition}
    p_M(B)\coloneqq(2\pi)^{-d| A|/2}(\det M)^{-1/2}
        \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}B^{\mathsf T}M^{-1}B\right)\;.
\end{equation}
The determinant square root is positive for positive real $M$ and is continued analytically on the accretive covariance domain.

Let $P_{\pi}$ be the matrix whose $bc$ entry is one when $b,c$ belong to the same block of a partition $\pi$ of $A$, and zero otherwise. Let $\mathcal K_A$ be the convex hull of these partition matrices. If $\pi_t$ is the partition into components of the forest edges with $w_e\geqslant t$, then $w^F=\int_0^1P_{\pi_t}\,\dd t\in \mathcal K_A$. Block restriction and convexity give $\lambda I\leqslant C_A(x)\leqslant \Lambda I$ throughout $\mathcal K_A$.

For the fixed integrand $F_JG_S$, its Gaussian integral is smooth on the open set $\{ x\, | \,C_A(x)>(\lambda/2)I\}$: the protected local factors are bounded, and derivatives of the density are polynomials times a uniformly integrable Gaussian on compact subsets. This set contains the compact set $\mathcal K_A$. A smooth multiplier with compact support inside this open set and equal to one near $\mathcal K_A$ gives a smooth extension by zero to the full interpolation space.

The Taylor forest formula applies to this extension. At the all-one matrix and at every $w^F$, its value and all the required derivatives agree with those of the original Gaussian integral. The extension therefore gives exactly \eqref{eq:marginal-forest-identity}; no hard cutoff or Wilson function is differentiated. This is the Taylor forest construction of Abdesselam--Rivasseau, Theorems III.1 and IV.5 and Section V.A \cite{AbdesselamRivasseau}.

Two bonds are also joined when they belong to the same selected label support; this finite-range graph is $Q_J$. A connected component of $F\cup Q_J$, together with its selected labels and forest edges, is a component label $\gamma$. Let $A_{\gamma},D_{\gamma},P_{\gamma},S_{\gamma},F_{\gamma}$ be these restrictions. Its scalar integration functional is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-component-functional}
    \mathcal I_{\gamma}[H]
        \coloneqq\int_{[0,1]^{F_{\gamma}}}\int
            F_{J_{\gamma}}(B)H(B)
            \left.\partial_{F_{\gamma}}p_{C_{A_{\gamma}}(x)}(B)
            \right|_{x= w^{F_{\gamma}}}
                \,\dd B\,\dd w\;.
\end{equation}

The covariance and every differentiated edge in \eqref{eq:marginal-forest-identity} are block diagonal across distinct components of $F\cup Q_J$. Their normalised densities, including determinants, consequently factor exactly into \eqref{eq:marginal-component-functional}. Every component uses the principal marginal of the same $C_T$; it is independent of the labels outside its carrier.

At the flat reference $C_T$ commutes with simultaneous constant conjugation. Principal restriction, scalar covariance interpolation, inversion and differentiation preserve this law. Every local scalar factor in $F_J$ is invariant as well. Thus each component integration is equivariant.

For $S_{\gamma}\ne \varnothing$, let $h_{\gamma}$ be the shortest cyclic interval of traversal positions containing $S_{\gamma}$, resolving ties by the first initial position encountered from the fixed contour base in its orientation. A singleton has an interval of length one. On a line the interval runs from the first to the last selected traversal.

Components whose intervals intersect are merged into webs; the web interval is their union, possibly the whole circle. This union is an interval because its interval-intersection graph is connected. Distinct web intervals are disjoint.

A web is integrated as the single closed source $G_{\cup_{\gamma\in W}S_{\gamma}}$ against the product of its component functionals. Its scalar activity is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-web-activity}
    z_W\coloneqq\left(\bigotimes_{\gamma\in W}\mathcal I_{\gamma}\right)
        \left[G_{\cup_{\gamma\in W}S_{\gamma}}\right]\;.
\end{equation}
The vacuum activity is $z_{\gamma}=\mathcal I_{\gamma}[1]$ when $S_{\gamma}=\varnothing$. Components inside a web have disjoint carriers. Distinct webs must also have disjoint contour intervals. Vacuum objects are incompatible only through intersection of their carriers with another object's carrier.

Independent constant conjugation in the component integrals and irreducibility give the integrated Schur factorisation for distinct webs. It is applied inside the closed Wilson contraction.

For the logarithm domain, each contour traversal carries a complex variable $t_a$, and $G_S$ is replaced by $(\prod_{a\in S}t_a)G_S$. The source polydisc is $| t_a|\leqslant 2$. Its factor $2^{| S|}$ is included in the constants of the source bounds below.

At zero source the numerator is $D_T$, and at $t_a=1$ it is $N_{C,T}$. The finite forest expansion and the unique component and web partitions consequently give
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-exact-gases}
    N_{C,T}=\Xi_{C,T},\qquad D_T=\Xi_{0,T},\qquad
    \mathcal W_T^{\circ}(C)=\frac{\Xi_{C,T}}{\Xi_{0,T}}\;.
\end{equation}
Both gases are sums over unordered compatible families of the activities just defined, with the empty family contributing one.

Conversely, let a compatible family of vacuum components and webs be given. Their constituent carriers are disjoint, so their label selections and forests have unambiguous unions. Every support edge and forest edge remains within its specified component. The component decomposition of this union recovers the original components, and the interval-intersection decomposition recovers precisely the webs, since distinct web intervals are disjoint. Thus the reassembly is inverse to the decomposition. If a web interval crosses the contour base, cyclicity of the trace moves that base between two web intervals before the Schur factorisation; the resulting scalar is unchanged.

\subsection{The Integrated Density Estimate}

Let a forest on $A$ be fixed, let $n=| A|$, and let $d_b$ be its vertex degrees. For an edge $e=\{ b,c\}$ with nonzero covariance block, the complex Cauchy radius is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-edge-radius}
    r_e\coloneqq\frac{\lambda}{8d_bd_c\| C_T(b,c)\|}\;.
\end{equation}
A zero covariance block gives a zero differentiated term. Only the forest variables are perturbed about $w^F$. The sum of the norms of the perturbation blocks in row $b$ is at most $\lambda/8$, since $\sum_{c:\{ b,c\}\in F}(d_bd_c)^{-1}\leqslant 1$. Thus the covariance perturbation has operator norm at most $\lambda/8$. If $M$ is any covariance on these Cauchy circles, then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-complex-density}
    \operatorname{Re}M\geqslant \frac{7\lambda}{8}I,
    \qquad \| M\|\leqslant \Lambda+\frac{\lambda}{8},
    \qquad
    \operatorname{Re}M^{-1}\geqslant
        \frac{7\lambda/8}{(\Lambda+\lambda/8)^2}I=\kappa_G I\;.
\end{equation}
The inverse bound follows from $\operatorname{Re}M^{-1}= M^{-*}(\operatorname{Re}M)M^{-1}$. The determinant branch is continued from the positive real covariance. Its modulus satisfies $|\det M|\geqslant (7\lambda/8)^{d n}$. Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-density-majorant}
    | p_M(B)|\leqslant
        (2\pi)^{-dn/2}(7\lambda/8)^{-dn/2}
            e^{-\kappa_G\| B\|^2/2}\;.
\end{equation}

Norm equivalence and a Gaussian exponential moment give a factor $C e^{-c r^2}$ for each distinct selected bad bond. Each regular vertex is bounded on its own cutoff by $C g_0(1+r)^3$, using \eqref{eq:perimeter-literal-local-bound}. The closed source with $q$ selected traversals has bound $(C_{\chi} g_0r)^q$; for $q=1$ it has the improved bound $C_{\chi} g_0^2r^2$, since $\dd\chi_{\id}=0$. These bounds are applied to the closed source inside the density integral.

Cauchy's formula and \eqref{eq:marginal-density-majorant} therefore bound the integrated term for a fixed component by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-fixed-forest-bound}
    K^{| A_{\gamma}|}
        \prod_{\{ b,c\}\in F_{\gamma}}
            \left(\frac{8d_bd_c}{\lambda}\| C_T(b,c)\|\right)
        \tau^{| D_{\gamma}|+| P_{\gamma}|+| S_{\gamma}|
            +\mathbf1_{\{| S_{\gamma}|=1\}}},
    \qquad
    \tau= C\left[g_0(1+r)^3+e^{-cr^2}\right]\;.
\end{equation}
Here and below $g_0$ is small enough that $\tau<1$ and the original chart condition holds. The same majorants multiply for a web.

For a component with exactly one source mark inside a larger web, the extra power comes from integrating that component first inside the closed contraction. Its matrix factor is a scalar by constant conjugation and irreducibility, and its scalar is the closed one-mark character difference. Components with two or more marks already supply two source powers.

The degree factors in \eqref{eq:marginal-fixed-forest-bound} are paid by spatial decay. The free-bond lattice has uniformly bounded polynomial volume growth of degree four, including on its finite tori. For $d$ distinct neighbours of a fixed bond, their distances have sum at least $c_1d^{5/4}-c_2d$. Hence, for each $\zeta>0$, a constant $K_{\zeta}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-degree-payment}
    d^d\leqslant K_{\zeta}^d
        \exp\left(\zeta\sum_{j=1}^d d_T(b,c_j)\right)\;.
\end{equation}
Indeed $d\log d$ is bounded by any fixed positive multiple of $d^{5/4}$ plus a linear function of $d$; here $0^0=1$. Taking $\zeta$ smaller than $\mu/4$ absorbs $\prod_b d_b^{d_b}$ into part of the covariance decay. The remaining forest edge weights are bounded by $K e^{-\mu d_T(b,c)/2}$, with a further positive part of the decay available for support-length weights.

On a carrier of $n$ bonds there are at most $2^{q_*n}$ choices of elementary labels. A selection covering that carrier contains at least $\lceil n/s_*\rceil$ labels. The edges of $Q_J$ have bounded range and bounded degree.

For fixed $J$ and a fixed graph $G= F\cup Q_J$, the edges of $F$ outside $Q_J$ are determined; its edges inside $Q_J$ have at most $2^{| Q_J|}$ choices. The support counts give $| Q_J|\leqslant q_*(s_*-1)n/2$; this exponential multiplicity is included in $K_1$ below.

Each forest edge weight is bounded by the following pair weight, and this weight is at least one on every edge of $Q_J$. Thus the forest sum is bounded, with that multiplicity, by a sum over connected graphs with pair weights
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-counting-weight}
    v(b,c)=\mathbf1_{\{ d_T(b,c)\leqslant R_*\}}
        +K e^{-\mu d_T(b,c)/4},
    \qquad \sup_b\sum_{c\ne b}v(b,c)= V_*<\infty\;.
\end{equation}
The unused graph edges cost at most $\prod_{b< c}(1+v(b,c))\leqslant e^{V_*n/2}$. Keeping one spanning tree gives the remaining tree sum. For $n\geqslant 2$ and a fixed root bond $b_0$, summing its possible distinct vertices gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-rooted-tree-count}
    \sum_{\substack{A\ni b_0\\| A|= n}}
        \sum_{T\ \mathrm{tree\ on}\ A}\prod_{\{ b,c\}\in T}v(b,c)
        \leqslant \frac{n^{n-2}}{(n-1)!}V_*^{n-1}\;.
\end{equation}
The factorial accounts for unordered nonroot vertices; the bound follows by summing their positions along a rooted labelled tree. The right-hand side is bounded exponentially in $n$.

Combining these payments yields convergent series bounded by constants times
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-load-series}
    \sum_{n\geqslant 1}K_1^n\tau^{\lceil n/s_*\rceil}= O(\tau),
    \qquad
    \sum_{n\geqslant 1}K_1^n\tau^{\max(2,\lceil n/s_*\rceil)}= O(\tau^2)\;.
\end{equation}
The first applies to vacuum components and the second to source components, rooted either at a spatial bond or at a specified source traversal. The coupling is chosen after the constants so that $K_1^{s_*}\tau$ is sufficiently small; exponential weights in the carrier size and in the sum of covariance-edge lengths remain available.

\subsection{Extent Weights and the Square Geometry}\label{sec:extent-weights}

The extent costs of a component, a web, and a cluster are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-extent}
    \ell(\gamma)\coloneqq| A_{\gamma}|+
        \sum_{\{ b,c\}\in F_{\gamma}}d_T(b,c),
    \qquad \ell(W)\coloneqq\sum_{\gamma\in W}\ell(\gamma),
    \qquad \ell(\Gamma)\coloneqq\sum_{p\in \Gamma}\ell(p)\;.
\end{equation}
A vacuum object uses its component cost. $A_p$ denotes an object's carrier and $H_p$ its contour interval length, with $H_p=0$ for vacuum objects.

On a straight line, connectivity of $F_{\gamma}\cup Q_{J_{\gamma}}$ gives $H_{\gamma}\leqslant c_h\ell(\gamma)$, since the support edges have length at most $R_*$ and the source positions are within $R_*$ of their supports; $c_h$ is fixed at \eqref{eq:marginal-hull-extent} below, where the square is treated, and the same constant covers the line, the interval length there being at most the spatial span of the marks plus one. ($H_p$, the contour interval length, is also called the contact-interval length below.)

Here the square $C_n$ has vertices $0,nLe_1,nL(e_1+e_2),nLe_2$ in a fixed lift, with all other coordinates zero. Its side length is $nL$ fine bonds, its physical perimeter is $4nL\varepsilon$, and its corners are coarse sites. The finite torus has fine periods $LK_i$, with $K_i\geqslant 3(n+2)$ and the native grid divisibilities. The limits taken below (the joint limit in $n$ and the periods of \eqref{eq:marginal-square-mass}, the torus limit at fixed $n$ and the iterated limit of the corner section) are over such compatible integers $n$ and periods. Between points of this square the periodic coordinate distances equal their distances in the stated lift. This fixes one coordinate plane, one position and one orientation.

An oriented square contour $C$ as chosen at the start of the paper, with coarse corners and sides along two coordinate directions, is a coarse translate of the square with vertices $0,nLe_{\mu},nL(e_{\mu}+e_{\nu}),nLe_{\nu}$, traversed in this cyclic order or in the reverse one (the base point does not affect $\chi(\operatorname{Hol})$). The permutation of the coordinate axes carrying $(e_{\mu},e_{\nu})$ to $(e_1,e_2)$, with the periods permuted accordingly, is a symmetry of the fine lattice, of the Wilson measure $\rho_0(U)\,\dd U$ and of every hypothesis on the periods (all are imposed on every period), so $\mathbb E_{\varepsilon}[W_{\chi}(C)]$ equals the expectation of a coarse translate of $C_n$, which is the contour admitted in Section~\ref{sec:c4c-1} and in (H3).

Reversing the orientation inverts the holonomy, and $\chi(U^{-1})=\overline{\chi(U)}$ for the character of a unitary representation, so the expectation of the reversed square is the complex conjugate of that of the original. Every statement below about $\mathbb E_{\varepsilon}[W_{\chi}(C_n)]$ therefore holds for every such square, up to complex conjugation for the reversed orientation.

Let $D$ be the maximum-norm diameter of a nonempty set of square contacts and let $s= nL$. If $D< s/2$, its contacts occupy one side or two adjacent sides near their common corner, and an arc of length at most $4D+1$ contains them. If $D\geqslant s/2$, the whole contour has length $4s\leqslant 8D$.

A connected support network for the component has length at most $R_*| A_{\gamma}|+\sum_{F_{\gamma}}d_T(b,c)$, and each contact is within $R_*$ of that network. With the stated bond-distance convention, $c_h=32(1+R_*)$ (the interval constant, italic subscript; distinct from the group constant $c_{\mathrm h}=\sqrt N$ of Appendix~\ref{app:background-estimates}) therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-hull-extent}
    H_{\gamma}\leqslant c_h\ell(\gamma),
    \qquad H_W\leqslant \sum_{\gamma\in W}H_{\gamma}
        \leqslant c_h\ell(W)\;.
\end{equation}
Let $d_C$ count the shortest number of traversal steps between two positions, cyclically for a square. For $\theta>0$, a position $a$ in $h_{\gamma}$ satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-hull-root}
    \mathbf1_{\{ a\in h_{\gamma}\}}
        \leqslant \sum_{b\in S_{\gamma}}
            e^{-\theta d_C(a,b)}e^{\theta H_{\gamma}}\;.
\end{equation}
The sum of $e^{-\theta d_C(a,b)}$ over all traversal positions is bounded by $1+2/(e^{\theta}-1)$, uniformly in the contour length. The already proved traversal-root load, with the extra extent weight, therefore gives an interval-root load of order $\tau^2$.

For a source component let $u_{\gamma}$ be the positive majorant on the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:marginal-fixed-forest-bound}, with the constants fixed there, and let $H_{\gamma}\coloneqq| h_{\gamma}|$ be its contact-interval length.

In the sum over webs, the indicator that their interval graph is connected is majorised by its spanning-tree sum. The rooted-tree recursion is bounded by $u_{\gamma} e^{aH_{\gamma}}$ whenever the interval-root load, with this extra weight, is at most $a$. This follows by iterating $T_{\gamma}= u_{\gamma}\exp(\sum_{\gamma':h_{\gamma'}\cap h_{\gamma}\ne \varnothing}T_{\gamma'})$ from $T_{\gamma}= u_{\gamma}$, since the sum in the exponent is bounded by $aH_{\gamma}$. Spatial incompatibilities only reduce this majorant. The resulting whole-web loads are $O(\tau^2)$.

Together with the vacuum load $O(\tau)$, they satisfy the hard-core polymer convergence criterion \cite{KoteckyPreiss}, with size equal to carrier size plus a small positive multiple of contour interval length. This proves absolute convergence of the connected logarithm of \eqref{eq:marginal-exact-gases} for sufficiently small fixed $g_0$. In particular the numerator has no zero on the source-scaling polydisc used by that expansion. Its logarithm is fixed by continuation from zero source, where numerator and denominator agree.

More explicitly, let $\beta\coloneqq\mu/(1024(1+c_h))$, $\eta=\mu/1024$, and $a(p)=| A_p|+\beta H_p$. The density and graph payments above remain valid after multiplying the component majorants by $e^{4| A_{\gamma}|+8\beta H_{\gamma}+8\eta\ell(\gamma)}$: the added edge exponent is smaller than the unused covariance decay, and the added carrier exponent only changes $K_1$. With $a=\beta$ in the web recursion and the remaining weights reserved for its interval-root conversion, there is a constant $C_*$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-weighted-loads}
    \begin{aligned}
        \sup_b\sum_{p\, | \,b\in A_p}
            | z_p| e^{2a(p)+2\eta\ell(p)}&\leqslant C_*\tau\;,\\
        \sup_a\sum_{W\, | \,a\in h_W}
            | z_W| e^{2a(W)+2\eta\ell(W)}&\leqslant C_*\tau^2\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
The source-only version of the first sum is also bounded by $C_*\tau^2$. The coupling $g_0$ is chosen after these constants so that $C_*\tau\leqslant 1/4$ and $C_*\tau^2\leqslant \beta/4$. Carrier intersection and interval intersection then give the criterion
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-KP-payment}
    \sum_{q\not \sim p}| z_q| e^{a(q)+\eta\ell(q)}
        \leqslant C_*\tau| A_p|+C_*\tau^2H_p
        \leqslant \frac{1}{4}a(p)\;.
\end{equation}
A cluster $\Gamma=(p_1,\ldots,p_j)$, with $j\geqslant 1$, is an ordered tuple of vacuum components or source webs with connected incompatibility graph; repetitions are allowed and an object is incompatible with itself. Its scalar weight is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-cluster-weight}
    \Phi_C(\Gamma)\coloneqq\frac{1}{j!}
        \left(\sum_{H\ \mathrm{connected\ on}\ \{1,\ldots,j\}}
            \prod_{\{ r,s\}\in H}(-\mathbf1_{\{ p_r\not \sim p_s\}})\right)
        \prod_{r=1}^j z_{p_r}\;.
\end{equation}
The pinned version used here retains an activity factor. Let $\widetilde z_p\coloneqq z_pe^{\eta\ell(p)}$, and let $m_p(\Gamma)$ count the occurrences of $p$ in the ordered cluster tuple. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-pinned-bound}
    \sum_{\Gamma} m_p(\Gamma)|\Phi_C(\Gamma)| e^{\eta\ell(\Gamma)}
        \leqslant | z_p| e^{\eta\ell(p)+a(p)}\;.
\end{equation}
For a fixed incompatibility graph on labelled vertices, the connected subgraphs are partitioned by their breadth-first spanning tree rooted at vertex one, with the least-labelled parent at the previous level. A tree's interval of subgraphs allows all edges within a level and the edges to the previous level whose other endpoint is no earlier than the chosen parent. These intervals partition the connected graphs. The alternating sum on each interval is zero or has modulus one. Therefore the absolute Ursell coefficient is bounded by the sum over its spanning trees.

The positive generating sum of rooted trees with root species $p$ and vertex weights $|\widetilde z_q|$ is the monotone limit of
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-pinned-recursion}
    T_p^{(0)}=|\widetilde z_p|,
    \qquad
    T_p^{(k+1)}=|\widetilde z_p|
        \exp\left(\sum_{q\not \sim p}T_q^{(k)}\right)\;.
\end{equation}

Permutation symmetry of the ordered tuple gives $\sum_{\Gamma} m_p(\Gamma)F(\Gamma)= j\sum_{\Gamma\, | \,p_1= p}F(\Gamma)$ at each fixed length $j$ for its symmetric weight $F$. Hence the factor $1/j!$ becomes $1/(j-1)!$, including repeated species. The exponential in \eqref{eq:marginal-pinned-recursion} assembles an unordered family of child trees, with its factorial for repeated choices; $T_p^{(k)}$ enumerates rooted trees of height at most $k$. Equation~\eqref{eq:marginal-KP-payment} implies inductively $T_p^{(k)}\leqslant |\widetilde z_p| e^{a(p)}$, proving \eqref{eq:marginal-pinned-bound}.

For a countable polymer family, the species are first restricted to a finite subset. The same upper bound holds for every such restriction, and monotone convergence of the positive majorants proves the pinned bound for the countable family.

The bound applies to the source objects meeting a fixed coarse contour segment $x$. Their weighted activity sum is bounded by the source-only loads in \eqref{eq:marginal-weighted-loads}. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-cluster-tail}
    \sum_{\Gamma\, | \,x\in J_{\Gamma}}
        |\Phi_C(\Gamma)| e^{\eta\ell(\Gamma)}
        \leqslant C\tau^2\;.
\end{equation}
Here $J_{\Gamma}$ consists of the coarse segments containing its source marks. A coarse segment contains $L$ fine traversal positions, which changes only the constant. The same proof applies on the infinite lattice, using its finite principal covariance marginals.

A spanning tree of $F_{\gamma}\cup Q_{J_{\gamma}}$ connects each component carrier. Its metric length is at most $R_*| A_{\gamma}|+\sum_{F_{\gamma}}d_T(b,c)$. Paths of length at most $R_*$ attach its source contacts; there are at most $q_*| A_{\gamma}|$ contacts. A web becomes connected after adjoining its contour intervals, whose total length is at most $c_h\ell(W)$ by \eqref{eq:marginal-hull-extent}. In a cluster, incompatible objects meet through carriers or contour intervals, so these networks form a connected union. The carrier bonds themselves add at most $| A_{\gamma}|$ per component, and conversion from maximum-norm distances to lattice path lengths costs at most four. Thus its length and diameter are bounded by $C_{\mathrm{net}}\ell(\Gamma)$ with $C_{\mathrm{net}}\coloneqq 8(1+R_*)(1+q_*+c_h)$. This remains an upper bound with repeated objects. Equation~\eqref{eq:marginal-cluster-tail} therefore controls spatial extent as well as contour span.

\subsection{The Perimeter Coefficient}

The infinite-lattice covariance is constructed from the same periodic block grid. Its finite principal marginals satisfy the same spectral and decay bounds, so the density, counting and weighted KP estimates above apply with the same constants.

For an orientation $v\in \mathscr V_{\square}=\{ e_1,e_2,-e_1,-e_2\}$, the straight line through the coarse origin in that orientation is divided into half-open segments of $L$ fine traversals, indexed by $\mathbb Z$. Every side of $C_n$ is a coarse translation of the corresponding oriented segment of this line. Each square traversal belongs to exactly one side and one such segment. The lattice spacing $\varepsilon$ is the fixed physical length of a fine bond.

$\Phi_v$ denotes the connected weight \eqref{eq:marginal-cluster-weight} on the straight line in orientation $v$.

For a finite set $S$ of traversal positions on the line, let $I$ be any finite oriented arc containing it. For $R\subseteq S$, let $u_a^R\coloneqq U_{g_0}(b_a)$ on $R$ and $u_a^R= U_0(b_a)$ otherwise, with $U_0=\id$. The closed relative source on the line is explicitly
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-line-source}
    G_S^v(B)=\sum_{R\subseteq S}(-1)^{| S|-| R|}
        \chi\left(\left(\prod_{a\in I}^{\longrightarrow}u_a^R(B)\right)
            P_{U_0}(I)^{-1}\right)\;.
\end{equation}
The arrow means order along the arc. The reference reverse transport closes the word, and extending the arc beyond its selected marks adds only identity factors in the reference gauge. This is the line version of the finite closed source definition used above.

Let $J_{\Gamma}\subset \mathbb Z$ be the set of coarse line segments containing at least one source mark of the cluster. The vacuum subtraction in $\log\Xi_C-\log\Xi_0$ retains exactly the clusters with $J_{\Gamma}\ne \varnothing$. Translation by one coarse segment preserves the reference construction. The absolutely convergent line density and its coefficient are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-full-perimeter}
    \boxed{\displaystyle
        \kappa_v(g_0)\coloneqq\sum_{\Gamma\, | \,0\in J_{\Gamma}}
                    \frac{\Phi_v(\Gamma)}{| J_{\Gamma}|},
        \qquad \delta m_v(g_0,\varepsilon)
            \coloneqq-\frac{\kappa_v(g_0)}{L\varepsilon}}
        \;.
\end{equation}
The factor $| J_{\Gamma}|^{-1}$ allocates each translated connected contribution once. The weights contain the full local exponentials and exact hard-cutoff factors. The weighted rooted estimate \eqref{eq:marginal-cluster-tail} proves absolute convergence and $|\kappa_v|\leqslant C\tau^2$.

\paragraph{Length Allocation and Corners.}
Let $I_m\coloneqq\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$. The infinite-lattice logarithm for the finite straight relative word of length $mL$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-finite-line-log}
    F_v(m)\coloneqq\sum_{\Gamma\, | \,\varnothing\ne J_{\Gamma}\subseteq I_m}
        \Phi_v(\Gamma)\;.
\end{equation}
It is the bulk limit of the logarithm of the same finite-word numerator divided by $D_T$. For fixed $m$, this follows by truncating \eqref{eq:marginal-cluster-tail}, taking the limit of finitely many covariance-marginal integrals, and then removing the truncation. Translation invariance gives the exact difference
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-line-endpoints}
    F_v(m)-m\kappa_v
        =-\sum_{x\in I_m}
            \sum_{\substack{\Gamma\, | \,x\in J_{\Gamma}\\
                                      J_{\Gamma}\not \subseteq I_m}}
                \frac{\Phi_v(\Gamma)}{| J_{\Gamma}|}\;.
\end{equation}
A cluster in the inner sum joins a source in segment $x$ to a source outside $I_m$. With $R_{\mathrm{end}}=2L+4R_*$, the network bound gives $C_{\mathrm{net}}\ell(\Gamma)\geqslant (L\min(x+1,m-x)-R_{\mathrm{end}})_+$, where $t_+\coloneqq\max(t,0)$. Applying \eqref{eq:marginal-cluster-tail} and summing that geometric tail yields
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-line-density-limit}
    | F_v(m)-m\kappa_v|\leqslant C\tau^2\;.
\end{equation}

For the square in the infinite-lattice reference, clusters whose source marks all lie on one side have exactly the corresponding line weights: their contact intervals stay on that side, their closed words have the same ordered nonidentity factors, and every local primitive is translated by a multiple of $L$. The Gaussian marginal is unchanged by this translation.

All other source clusters touch at least two sides. Each such cluster is allocated over its source segments with the weight $| J_{\Gamma}|^{-1}$. A root segment at distance $j$ from its nearest corner can be joined to another side only by a cluster with $C_{\mathrm{net}}\ell(\Gamma)\geqslant (Lj-R_{\mathrm{end}})_+$. Thus the sum over mixed-side clusters is bounded by $C\tau^2\sum_{j\geqslant 0}e^{-c'j}$, with $c'\coloneqq\eta L/C_{\mathrm{net}}$ (the extent weight $e^{\eta\ell(\Gamma)}$ of \eqref{eq:marginal-cluster-tail}; the factor $e^{\eta R_{\mathrm{end}}/C_{\mathrm{net}}}$ is absorbed in $C$). With $\widehat F_{\square}(n)$ denoting its absolutely convergent infinite-lattice connected sum, this proves
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-square-corners}
    \left|\widehat F_{\square}(n)
        -\sum_{v\in \mathscr V_{\square}}F_v(n)\right|
        \leqslant C\tau^2,
    \qquad
    \left|\widehat F_{\square}(n)
        -n\sum_{v\in \mathscr V_{\square}}\kappa_v\right|
        \leqslant C\tau^2\;.
\end{equation}
The bounded corner contribution is extracted in Section~\ref{sec:marginal-corner}.

\paragraph{The Buffered Finite-Torus Limit.}
The perimeter coefficient also follows along the stated buffered tori. Let $R$ be an integer extent cutoff. A cluster rooted at a specified source segment with $\ell(\Gamma)\leqslant R$ has all its sites and marks in a neighbourhood of radius $C_{\mathrm{net}}R+L+2R_*$ in fine-lattice units around that segment. There are finitely many such cluster shapes, including multiplicities: each object has extent at least one, so a tuple has at most $R$ objects. Away from the square corners by more than $\left\lceil\frac{C_{\mathrm{net}}R+2L+2R_*}{L}\right\rceil$ coarse segments, these are the same shapes as on the corresponding straight line.

Each such root is translated to segment zero. Let $\epsilon_R(T)$ be the sum, over the four orientations and these finitely many shapes, of $|\Phi^T_v(\Gamma)-\Phi_v(\Gamma)|/| J_{\Gamma}|$. The finite-torus weight here is the same finite Gaussian-marginal integral on the translated sites. For large enough periods the shape embeds without wraparound. Periodisation gives entrywise convergence of all its covariance blocks, uniformly under the allowed coarse translations. The accretive density bound supplies a common integrable majorant for its Cauchy derivatives, so each integral and each finite product defining the cluster weight converges. Consequently $\epsilon_R(T)\to0$ as the shortest period tends to infinity, for every fixed $R$.

The finite-square logarithm is allocated over its source segments. The clusters omitted by the extent truncation cost at most $C\tau^2e^{-\eta R}$ per root. There are at most $cR$ corner-near roots per side, and each has load at most $C\tau^2$. Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-buffered-density}
    \left|\frac{1}{4n}\log\frac{N_{C_n,T}}{D_T}
        -\frac{1}{4}\sum_{v\in \mathscr V_{\square}}\kappa_v\right|
        \leqslant C\tau^2\left(\frac{R}{n}+e^{-\eta R}\right)
            +\epsilon_R(T)\;.
\end{equation}
The limit is taken first in $n$ and the compatible buffered periods with $R$ fixed, then in $R\to\infty$. Every logarithm in this limit is the analytic branch continued along $t_a= t$, $0\leqslant t\leqslant 1$, from the value zero of the logarithm of the ratio at $t=0$.

With the cutoff index restored, $\kappa_v^{\sigma}$ is the absolutely convergent line sum \eqref{eq:marginal-full-perimeter} with the prescription \eqref{eq:marginal-two-cutoffs}. For each $\sigma\in \{\mathrm{op},\mathrm{HS}\}$, the flat square perimeter coefficient exists and is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:marginal-square-mass}
    \boxed{\displaystyle
        \delta m^{\sigma}(g_0,\varepsilon)
            \coloneqq-\frac{1}{4L\varepsilon}
                \sum_{v\in \mathscr V_{\square}}\kappa_v^{\sigma}(g_0)
            =-\lim_{n\to\infty}
                \frac{1}{4nL\varepsilon}
                    \log\frac{N_{C_n,T_n}^{\sigma}}{D_{T_n}^{\sigma}}}
        \;.
\end{equation}
Reversing a finite relative path conjugates its character, and translation by its coarse length identifies it with the oppositely oriented reference path. All other factors of the weights (the Gaussian density and its forest derivatives, $f_v$, $h_b$ and $\theta$) are real, the reindexing $a\mapsto-a-1$ carries the $-v$ line onto the reverse of the $v$ line with the stencils, protected boxes, intervals and incompatibilities in bijection, and $\kappa_v$ is an absolutely convergent sum, so $\kappa_{-v}=\overline{\kappa_v}$. Hence the square coefficient is real.

\section{The Corner Coefficient in the Same First Step}
\label{sec:marginal-corner}

The lattice spacing, character, reconstruction, and cutoff prescription $\sigma$ are those of Section~\ref{sec:marginal-perimeter}, and the coupling is below the common minimum of the straight and bent-path smallness thresholds of this section and the regional thresholds of Proposition~\ref{prop:regional-square-extraction}, chosen after all chart radii and majorant constants. All limits in this section vary reference contours and enclosing tori at this one RG step. The coefficients below use $N_{C,T}^{\sigma}$ and $D_T^{\sigma}$ of \eqref{eq:marginal-literal-ratio}; $\sigma$ is suppressed until the conclusion.

$C_{\infty}=\mathsf H_{\infty}^{-1}$ is the free-field covariance on $\ell^2(E_{*,\infty};\mathfrak g)$, constructed in \eqref{eq:bulk-neumann-inverse}; it is distinct from the reconstructed fine-field covariance $\mathsf K_{\infty}=\mathsf C_{\infty} C_{\infty}\mathsf C_{\infty}^*$.

The countable primitive index family $\mathcal V_{\infty}$ consists of labels $(0,\alpha)$, $(1,b)$ and $(2,c)$ for the functions $v_{\alpha},j_b,d_c$ in \eqref{eq:perimeter-literal-local-terms}. Here $b$ ranges over positive fine bonds, $c$ over positive coarse bonds, and $\alpha$ over positive plaquettes and the mean-transport pairs $(y,x)$ with $y\in L\mathbb Z^4$ and $x\in\mathcal B_y\setminus\{ y\}$. These are exactly the infinite-lattice translates of the finitely many local templates modulo the coarse grid.

\subsection{A Local Corner Subtraction}

Let $v,w\in \mathscr V_{\square}$ be perpendicular incoming and outgoing orientations. For $a\in \mathbb Z$, the bent reference path has fine vertices and oriented bonds
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corner-bent-path}
    x_a^{v,w}=
    \begin{cases}
        av,&a<0,\\
        aw,&a\geqslant 0,
    \end{cases}
    \qquad b_a^{v,w}=(x_a^{v,w},x_{a+1}^{v,w})\;.
\end{equation}
Its coarse segment $j\in \mathbb Z$ contains the fine traversal indices $jL,\ldots,(j+1)L-1$. Thus the bend is at a coarse site, between segments $-1$ and $0$.

For every finite set of selected traversals, the closed relative source is \eqref{eq:marginal-line-source} on the corresponding finite arc of this bent path, with the same local vertices, protected cutoffs, and Gaussian principal marginals. Its components and webs are those of \eqref{eq:marginal-component-functional}--\eqref{eq:marginal-web-activity}, with ordinary intervals in the ordered traversal indices, and its connected weight $\Phi_{v,w}(\Gamma)$ is \eqref{eq:marginal-cluster-weight}. The set $J_{\Gamma}\subset \mathbb Z$ again records the coarse segments containing source marks. Vacuum-only clusters are excluded. These definitions involve finite closed contractions and finite-dimensional integrals only, even on the infinite reference path.

The density, label-counting and KP estimates of Section~\ref{sec:marginal-perimeter} apply to this path with enlarged fixed constants. Indeed, it has no repeated traversal, and the path distance between two of its points is at most twice their maximum-norm spatial distance. Each ray is part of one of the two straight lines, so at most $2q_*$ primitive or source labels meet any bond; the support sizes $s_*$ and ranges $R_*$ are unchanged. Thus the original counting proof applies with $q_*'=2q_*$, and the interval/extent bound holds with $c_h'=2c_h$. The resulting rooted estimate is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corner-bent-tail}
    \sum_{\Gamma\, | \,j\in J_{\Gamma}}
        |\Phi_{v,w}(\Gamma)| e^{\eta'\ell(\Gamma)}
        \leqslant C\tau^2\;.
\end{equation}

Let $\beta'\coloneqq\mu/(2048(1+c_h'))$ and $\eta'=\eta/2$. The index-distance conversion \eqref{eq:marginal-hull-root} is unchanged, since the traversal indices still form $\mathbb Z$ and the sum of its geometric kernel is $1+2/(e^{\theta}-1)$. The carrier-root and interval-root loads therefore obey \eqref{eq:marginal-weighted-loads} with the bent path, size $a'(p)=| A_p|+\beta'H_p$, exponent $\eta'$ and a fixed enlarged constant $C_*'$ obtained from the same label and positive-tree sums with $q_*'$. The coupling satisfies $C_*'\tau\leqslant 1/4$ and $C_*'\tau^2\leqslant \beta'/4$. The incompatibility sum is then at most $a'(p)/4$, and the pinned proof \eqref{eq:marginal-pinned-bound}--\eqref{eq:marginal-pinned-recursion} gives \eqref{eq:corner-bent-tail}, for both cutoff choices.

The relative word transforms by conjugation at its base when field and reference are transformed together, and its character, component-integrated closed contractions and scalar cluster weights are gauge invariant.

The rooted density and its straight reference are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corner-rooted-density}
    a_{v,w}(j)\coloneqq\sum_{\Gamma\, | \,j\in J_{\Gamma}}
        \frac{\Phi_{v,w}(\Gamma)}{| J_{\Gamma}|},
    \qquad
    k_{v,w}(j)\coloneqq
    \begin{cases}
        \kappa_v,&j<0,\\
        \kappa_w,&j\geqslant 0.
    \end{cases}
    \;.
\end{equation}
The straight densities are those of \eqref{eq:marginal-full-perimeter}. The local corner coefficient is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corner-local-extraction}
    \boxed{\displaystyle
        \zeta_{v,w}\coloneqq\sum_{j\in \mathbb Z}
            \left(a_{v,w}(j)-k_{v,w}(j)\right),
        \qquad z_{v,w}\coloneqq\exp(\zeta_{v,w})}\;.
\end{equation}

A cluster with all source marks at negative indices has exactly the weight of the same cluster on the incoming straight line: its ordered nonidentity factors, source stencils, ordinary intervals, local vacuum factors and Gaussian marginals agree. The same holds on the positive half-line with orientation $w$. Vacuum carriers may cross the bend. Consequently only clusters with source marks on both sides of index zero survive the difference of the rooted sums. On the straight side of the subtraction these are the straight clusters straddling the same cut.

A surviving cluster rooted in segment $j$ has extent at least $c| j|-C_0$, with $c\coloneqq L/(2C_{\mathrm{net}})$ and $C_0= R_*/C_{\mathrm{net}}$, since its connected support/interval network reaches the other half-line, so has length at least $L| j|-2R_*$, while the bent-path network constant ($C_{\mathrm{net}}$ with $q_*'$, $c_h'$) is at most $2C_{\mathrm{net}}$. The rooted bound, with part of its extent weight retained, therefore gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corner-localisation-bound}
    | a_{v,w}(j)-k_{v,w}(j)|
        \leqslant C\tau^2e^{-c| j|},
    \qquad
    |\zeta_{v,w}|\leqslant C\tau^2,
    \qquad | z_{v,w}-1|\leqslant C\tau^2\;.
\end{equation}
This proves absolute convergence and localisation at the corner.

Let $J_{\Gamma}^-\coloneqq J_{\Gamma}\cap\mathbb Z_{<0}$ and $J_{\Gamma}^+= J_{\Gamma}\cap\mathbb Z_{\geqslant 0}$. In each of the following three sums, the cluster has both $J_{\Gamma}^-\ne \varnothing$ and $J_{\Gamma}^+\ne \varnothing$, and its weight is that of the indicated bent or straight path. Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corner-mixed-cluster-formula}
    \begin{aligned}
        \zeta_{v,w}
            &=\sum_{\Gamma}^{v,w}\Phi_{v,w}(\Gamma)
                -\sum_{\Gamma}^{v}
                    \frac{| J_{\Gamma}^-|}{| J_{\Gamma}|}\Phi_v(\Gamma)\\
            &\quad-\sum_{\Gamma}^{w}
                    \frac{| J_{\Gamma}^+|}{| J_{\Gamma}|}\Phi_w(\Gamma)\;.
    \end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Indeed, summing the rooted allocations gives one for a mixed bent cluster and the displayed fractions for the two missing straight half-line contributions. Each sum is absolutely convergent by \eqref{eq:corner-bent-tail} and the distance-to-cut payment. In particular the corner factor includes the straight-edge endpoint deficits as well as interactions joining the two perpendicular rays.

\subsection{Identification with the Square Constant}

For a fixed positive integer $n$, let $\widehat F_{\square}(n)$ be the infinite-lattice connected sum over clusters with source marks on $C_n$, with its fixed cyclic traversal order and base, and let $F_{\square,\infty}(n)$ be the bulk-limit logarithm, whose existence is proved below.

The connected sum is allocated over the $4n$ coarse source segments by $| J_{\Gamma}|^{-1}$. Its absolute convergence follows from \eqref{eq:marginal-cluster-tail}. The same bound holds uniformly on all compatible tori, which satisfy $K_i\geqslant 3(n+2)$, so the square geometry and weighted KP payment used to prove that bound have their original constants, including at the corners.

Both connected sums are truncated to $\ell(\Gamma)\leqslant R$. Once the shortest fine period exceeds a fixed multiple of $nL+R+R_*$, each such rooted cluster has a unique lift through its source root to the fixed neighbourhood of the lifted square. Its connected support/interval network has length at most a fixed multiple of $R$, so a network winding around a torus cannot occur in this truncation. The primitive functions and supports agree after lifting. The cyclic interval rule and its tie-breaking base depend only on the fixed ordered list of square traversals, so they agree as well, including intervals crossing the base.

There are finitely many lifted shapes, labels and multiplicities: the root belongs to a finite contour, the extent bounds all spatial displacements and the number of component and cluster occurrences, and each site has finitely many primitive labels.

Covariance entries converge by the periodisation of $\mathsf H_{\infty}^{-1}$ (Appendix~\ref{app:flat-covariance}: the periodisation of the free inverse solves the torus inverse equation, the paragraph preceding \eqref{eq:bulk-periodisation}, and the image bound \eqref{eq:bulk-image-error}, displayed there for $\mathsf K$, holds for $\mathsf H_{\infty}^{-1}$ by the same argument from the decay of its entries established before \eqref{eq:bulk-kernel-decay}). For each shape, the differentiated Gaussian density majorant \eqref{eq:marginal-density-majorant} is integrable and uniform in the torus. Dominated convergence therefore gives convergence of every component integral, web activity and finite product in its cluster weight. Let $\mathscr G_{n,R}$ be this finite set of lifted ordered clusters with at least one source mark, and let
\begin{equation}\label{eq:corner-finite-shape-difference}
    \epsilon_{n,R}(T)\coloneqq\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathscr G_{n,R}}
        |\Phi_{\square}^T(\Gamma)-\Phi_{\square}^{\infty}(\Gamma)|\;.
\end{equation}
For the domination just used, every fixed shape has $r_e^{-1}\leqslant 8d_bd_cA/\lambda$ in \eqref{eq:marginal-edge-radius}, uniformly in $T$.
